ideas.name: Simple-looking systems can compute anything
ideas.statement: Even programs that look structurally simple can carry out computation as sophisticated as any other process, so their behavior cannot generally be predicted except by actually running them.

occurrences.quote: even programs (or fragments of them) that are very simple in their structure can end up doing computation that is in a sense as sophisticated as anything
occurrences.reasoning: states the core claim that simplicity of structure does not imply simplicity of behavior

occurrences.quote: if one runs this machine for inputs from 0 to 14 everything works just fine—but suddenly at n = 15, instead of giving output 15 + 1 = 16, the machine gives 20!
occurrences.reasoning: gives a concrete case where a tiny machine's behavior outruns the simple rule we expected

ideas.name: Pockets of reducibility survive inside irreducibility
ideas.statement: Even when a system's overall behavior cannot be predicted without running it, there will always be some specific facts or properties about it that can still be guaranteed in advance.

occurrences.quote: There are—as we'll discuss—necessarily "pockets of computational reducibility" in which we can expect to make progress.
occurrences.reasoning: introduces the concept that guarantees are still possible despite general unpredictability

occurrences.quote: One important feature of computational irreducibility is that whenever it's present, there must also be pockets of computational reducibility present.
occurrences.reasoning: states the principle directly as a general law

occurrences.quote: One can think of proofs as taking advantage of pockets of computational reducibility, to provide finite summaries of infinite things.
occurrences.reasoning: connects the concept to why finite proofs of correctness can exist at all

ideas.name: A bug only exists relative to a chosen specification
ideas.statement: Whether some behavior counts as a bug depends entirely on what simpler standard (a formula, a restated program, a rule like 'never run out of memory') you are comparing the program against, not on anything intrinsic to the code.

occurrences.quote: To tell if a program has a bug we have to know what the program is supposed to do—or is not supposed to do. And for this we have to have some kind of precise specification.
occurrences.reasoning: states directly that bugs are defined only relative to an external specification

occurrences.quote: There are several different types of specifications that end up being used.
occurrences.reasoning: shows that many different kinds of standards can play the specification role, reinforcing relativity of the bug concept

occurrences.quote: whatever constraint we give, there'll somehow always be machines that will insidiously escape it
occurrences.reasoning: shows the pattern holding across many different specification types, generalizing the idea

ideas.name: Seeing the whole computation beats summarizing it
ideas.statement: The best practical defense against bugs is to make the entire unfolding process of a computation visible to human perception, rather than relying on summary statistics or partial descriptions, because full visibility can sometimes let you directly see that no bug is possible.

occurrences.quote: the most important thing is to try to "see inside" what the program is doing, in as complete but human accessible a way as possible
occurrences.reasoning: states the practical strategy directly

occurrences.quote: If the behavior of a cellular automaton is "visually simple", we can immediately tell that it won't show bugs.
occurrences.reasoning: shows how visual completeness yields certainty that statistics alone couldn't

occurrences.quote: even tiny fragments of programs can be run on their own, giving one at least the raw material to "see in detail what a program is doing"
occurrences.reasoning: extends the visibility strategy to a language-design feature that enables it

ideas.name: Proving correctness costs the same unbounded effort as running the program
ideas.statement: Searching for a formal proof that a program behaves a certain way is not a shortcut around computational irreducibility: it takes a similarly unbounded amount of work, and when the claim is false, no amount of searching ever produces a proof.

occurrences.quote: we don't get any fundamental advantage by trying to make a proof rather than just running the Turing machine. In both cases we have to expend a potentially unbounded amount of computational effort.
occurrences.reasoning: states explicitly that proof search and exhaustive computation are equally costly

occurrences.quote: But now—however far we go—we never find a proof
occurrences.reasoning: shows the practical consequence: searching forever in a buggy machine's case yields nothing

ideas.name: Total predictability makes running a program pointless
ideas.statement: If you could fully foresee everything a program would do, there would be no reason to actually run it — you could just write down the answer directly; so any program worth running must have some unforeseeable part, which tends to drag in a lot of unforeseeability.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: This is the hinge that explains why bugs and computational usefulness are two sides of the same coin, rather than something to be engineered away.

occurrences.quote: if you can completely foresee what a program will do, what's the point of running it? Why not, in effect, just immediately "write down the answer", without ever having to run the program?
occurrences.reasoning: states the tradeoff between usefulness and predictability directly

occurrences.quote: Computational irreducibility is in a sense what makes computation powerful. But it's also what makes it unpredictable.
occurrences.reasoning: reaffirms that the same property that gives programs their power is what makes bugs inevitable

ideas.name: Testing many cases cannot rule out rare, arbitrarily hidden bugs
ideas.statement: Generalizing from many successful test cases to a universal rule fails in the presence of computational irreducibility, because a bug can be made as rare and as deeply buried as one likes, so no finite amount of sampling guarantees it has been found.

occurrences.quote: the number of samples might just not be large enough to ever hit a bug—given the density of bugs that are present.
occurrences.reasoning: makes explicit that sample size versus bug rarity determines detection, not certainty

ideas.name: Mathematics mostly avoids ruliology's bugs by staying human-scale
ideas.statement: Mainstream pure mathematics largely escapes the rampant surprises of computational irreducibility not because its subject matter is immune to it, but because mathematicians deliberately focus on human-graspable structures that happen to sit in reducible pockets; experimental mathematics, which samples broadly instead, runs into the same irreducibility and surprises as ruliology.

occurrences.quote: pure mathematics as it's normally practiced tends to concentrate on what amount to more "human-level" questions, that in effect exist in pockets of computational reducibility, that avoid the generic computational irreducibility of ruliology
occurrences.reasoning: states explicitly why ordinary mathematics mostly dodges ruliology-style bugs

occurrences.quote: somehow in the mainstream of pure mathematics, such issues are not very common
occurrences.reasoning: names the puzzle that the idea then resolves

ideas.name: Good language design hides irreducibility inside primitives
ideas.statement: A well-designed programming language packs most of the hard, unpredictable computation into its built-in primitives, so that the parts a person actually writes stay close to human intention and are less likely to misbehave.

occurrences.quote: What a well-designed language does is to provide as primitives lumps of computational work that are things humans typically actually want.
occurrences.reasoning: states the mechanism by which language design reduces bug propensity

occurrences.quote: most of the computational irreducibility has been packed into the primitives of the language, so that what's left over is the part that's accessible to us humans
occurrences.reasoning: explicitly locates where the irreducibility goes and why what remains is tractable

occurrences.quote: in Wolfram Language it's the short program that's the one that does what you want, without what you consider bugs.
occurrences.reasoning: gives the practical corollary that shortness in a good language correlates with correctness
